To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) a disease signature is the set of all possible exposures to a disease that can occur in a population; (b) an outbreak is an incident of spatial and temporal exposure spread of a disease signature; and (c) the outbreak decomposition model provides a means to understand, estimate and correct for reporting errors in disease surveillance.
we have developed a new model of disease spread that allows us to differentiate outbreak scenarios and estimate and correct for reporting error.

(i) the sequential combinatorial approach to outbreak decomposition is mathematically rigorous and provides a new way of understanding disease spread; (ii) this approach is useful in identifying the likely source and spread of disease in a population, and in estimating the likely number of cases of disease that were unreported; and (iii) this approach can be used to identify the most probable scenario for disease spread in the MA 1995 waterborne disease outbreak.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a rigorous mathematical model of disease spread and its application to the understanding of outbreaks of disease.
the development of a rigorous, mathematical, epidemiological framework for disease outbreak decomposition.
developing a new mathematical perspective on disease outbreak decomposition, and the application of this perspective to the study of real-world disease surveillance data.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the outbreak signature of an epidemic is the result of the combined effects of disease spread within and across populations and that the outbreak is the result of an epidemic of disease spread across populations.
the model we have developed is a powerful new tool for the understanding and analysis of disease outbreaks.
the MA 1995 outbreak is most probably a combination of a single outbreak in a single population and an unrelated outbreak in another population.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
our model is able to identify the likely source of an outbreak, and the likely population(s) that were exposed, in a more sensitive way than previous models have been able to.
we are able to provide a new, more sensitive, definition for the term 'outbreak'.

we have developed a new model of disease outbreak that is based on the mathematical properties of the epidemiological process, rather than the more common, and more subjective, statistical properties.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a simple model of disease spread, combined with a rigorous definition of an outbreak, can be used to understand and correct for reporting errors in disease surveillance data.

the use of a sequential model of disease spread, in conjunction with a population specific'signature', allows us to understand, and in many cases, correct for the reporting error inherent in the surveillance of disease outbreaks.

the mathematical modelling of disease outbreaks should be done using a rigorous definition of an outbreak, which we have proposed here, and that the modelling of disease outbreaks in populations should be done in the context of the population's disease signature.
